progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From B10: co-dominance, roan Shorthorn cattle (red C^R C^R, roan C^R C^W, white C^W C^W), the heterozygote looks different from both homozygotes. From B9: dominant, recessive, genotype and phenotype, a ratio is a chance per offspring and large samples come closer to it, Tt and tt notation with tall and short peas. From B8: crossing over swaps segments between homologous chromosomes. From B7: sickle cell begins with one base change, GAG to GTG on the coding strand. From B4: DNA bases A, T, C and G. Year 10 percentages. Not assumed: frequency as a defined measure, denominators, allele frequency, gene pool, SNP, association, sampling limits.
progression.startsWith: A sourced sample reports characteristics or variants. The video opens: Here's a herd of a hundred Shorthorn cattle. Sixty-four are red, thirty-two are roan, and four are white.
progression.stopsAfter: calculating the frequency of a characteristic as a count over the stated total, and presenting it as a table and a bar chart; calculating an allele frequency by counting copies (two per individual for an autosomal gene); explaining why a recessive phenotype frequency gives only the homozygous recessive genotype frequency, because carriers look like dominant homozygotes; describing a SNP as a one-base difference at a known position, each version an allele, and saying that reading both copies shows the genotype directly; saying that most SNPs change nothing but some change a protein; calculating a SNP allele frequency from genotype counts; comparing two groups to identify a trend and calling it an association, not a cause, with the reason (a nearby DNA difference inherited with it); explaining why one SNP cannot show relatedness; naming sample limits (size, representation, consistent categories); applying all of it to unseen clover leaf-mark counts and unseen SNP genotype counts.
progression.nextLesson: collecting and presenting frequency data yourself (route entry bio-m5-p03), then DNA sequencing and profiling (bio-m5-b12).

teaching.task: How do you work out how common a characteristic or an allele is in a population, and what can SNP data, and their limits, tell you?
teaching.causalExplanation: Causes: why 4% and 36% are wrong (copies, not animals, 3); why looks fail under complete dominance (carriers look like TT, 4); why reading DNA shows carriers (both copies read, 5); why most SNPs change nothing (non-coding DNA, 6); why an association need not be a cause (close neighbours inherited together, 8); why one SNP proves little (thousands of other differences, 9); why small samples mislead (they bounce, 10). Visible case: one herd, one pea field, one aligned strip, one pair of groups. Video advantage: the herd sorts itself; every allele pours into the pool bar and the white ones light by source; the SNP column is found by a scan; sample dots bounce live. Thinking opportunities: two unseen items with every count on screen. Reading load: one board at a time; scene 3 is the densest frame (grid, pool bar, two working lines), and the grid shrinks before the pool bar fills.
teaching.conversationalApproach: Conversational, one board at a time, causes before names. Scene 2 shows the count over the total before the word "frequency". Scene 3 shows two copies per animal before the word "allele frequency". Scene 5 shows the one differing column before naming the SNP, and glosses "single nucleotide" and "polymorphism". Scene 8 shows the two group bars before the word "association". Analogy: None manufactured. The herd is the concrete case for counting, and the aligned DNA rows are the concrete case for SNPs.
teaching.openingDecision: Thirty-six per cent? Hold that thought, because the answer is neither.
teaching.understandingCheck: 12a uses the site's earlobe item numbers on a non-human trait, the white clover V leaf mark (Revision 2; counts given; frequencies, comparison and one limitation): it tests the denominator trap and a real limitation. 12c is a SNP genotype count (find the allele frequency; then judge whether an association shows cause): it transfers "count alleles, not people" to new numbers and tests association against cause. Each ends "Pause here to answer." with a 10 s countdown; each card stays on screen during and after the countdown. Each feedback is brief (about 25 to 30 s): answer, key reason, short working on the card, one crossed-out classic mistake. No mark-allocation talk.
teaching.curriculumScope: "collect, record and present data to represent frequencies of characteristics in a population, in order to identify trends, patterns, relationships and limitations in data, for example: examining frequency data; analysing single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)". Route actions B-frequency-collection and B-frequency-analysis (ledger row p1060, shared with bio-m5-p03). This video presents and analyses data; it does not evidence learner collection, which P03 owns. Update ledger row p1060 (analysis and presentation part) when this design passes review.

design.visualSystem: Three boards, one at a time. (1) The count board (scenes 1 to 4, 10): the sample on the left as a 10 x 10 grid of small painted plates (cattle or peas), a tally table in the middle (category, count, out of, per cent; computed), a bar chart on the right (bars draw from the table; y axis "per cent of cattle counted" or "per cent of alleles"; every bar labelled with its value). Under it, the gene pool bar (scene 3): each animal's two allele chips pour into one long bar of 200 cells, red and white chips sorted to each end, with the count computed. (2) The read strip (scenes 5 to 9): rows of coded base tiles in B4's `BasePiece` look, two rows per sample (one per copy), aligned; a column highlight computes the differing position; a genotype tag at the end of each pair. Samples are coded ID cards ("sample 1"), never people. (3) The group panel (scenes 8, 9): two allele-bead groups (patients, controls) with frequency bars computed as hits divided by twice the number of people. Amber is the emphasis colour only, as in B9 and B10. Letters for bases are printed in a serif capital on the tiles; base colour is never the only cue.
design.transitionPlan: The herd grid fills and sorts itself by coat colour; the sorted grid slides left and shrinks beside the tally table and bar chart; the gene pool bar pours the allele chips for the copy count; the grid and bar fall away for the pea field; the read strip replaces the count board for the SNP scenes; the group panel carries association and the marker; the bouncing sample dots return to the count board for the limits; the memory aids and the decision chips follow; each attempt clears the board to one card and the feedback shrinks the card to a strip while the working writes on; scene crossfade with settle.
